name: Gareth Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach history at St Columba's, a small church secondary school in a farming town, about four hundred pupils, and we start every day with an assembly and a prayer. I teach the Romans to the eleven-year-olds and the two world wars to the fifteen-year-olds. My favourite thing is taking a class to the war memorial on the green and having them find their own surname on it. The tiring bit is the reports, and the endless forms about everything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Grace, who's a receptionist at the dental surgery on Bridge Street, and we're getting married next August at the church where my grandparents married. We rent a small cottage from a farmer, and I'm on lower pay because St Columba's is a small school with a tight budget. We've got less than a month of money saved, and most of what we save goes to the wedding. There's no other secondary school within twenty miles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and good. A lot of people were selling something and it didn't work out. I'd say it at the school gate and after church, but I don't go online much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relieved, but money's tight whatever AI does. The wedding's costing more than we planned, the cottage rent went up in spring, and I'm still on a low point. Nothing changing means nothing gets easier either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching exactly as I do now, with my own notes and my own worksheets. I'd ask the head about running the school's history club for a small allowance. And Grace and I would cut the wedding guest list from a hundred and twenty to ninety, which we've been arguing about anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but tired. Like the end of the autumn term, you're fine, you just need Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you use your own notes. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A filing box for each year group, handwritten and typed notes I've built up over five years. Some of the sheets are from my old history teacher, Mr Dunn, who gave me his box when he retired. I'd sooner use that than anything a computer makes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace say about the guest list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say we can't leave out her cousins, and she'd be right. We'll probably cut my side instead, my dad's friends from the bowls club. My fiancée Grace always wins these, and she's usually right.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because many people were selling something.
I'd say it at the **school gate** and after church, not online.
think: He's **relieved**, but money is tight regardless of AI.
The **wedding** and a spring rent rise mean nothing gets easier.
do: Keep teaching with his **own notes** and worksheets.
Ask the head about a **history club** allowance.
Cut the **wedding guest list** from a hundred and twenty to ninety.
feel: **Steady** but tired, like needing Christmas at the end of term.
S0.quote: Nothing changing means nothing gets easier either.
fieldNote: Gareth trusts **handed-down materials** from his old teacher over anything digital.
His pressure is the **wedding** and rent, not technology.
He defers to his fiancée with **good humour**.

steps.text: Keep teaching from his own handwritten history notes
Run the school's history club for a small allowance
Cut the wedding guest list to ninety

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful, because a school isn't a business and children aren't customers. I'd say parents should decide what their children use, not tech firms. I wouldn't be against people choosing it, but I'd want a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried, but more for Grace than me. Booking and answering patients is exactly what the card says AI takes first, and the dental surgery would swap her for a screen the moment it's cheaper. For me, history is mostly reading, writing and marking, so I think the school would push me to use AI for all of it, and maybe merge classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what the school asks before touching any of it. Grace and I would move the wedding to a smaller do in the church hall to save about four thousand pounds. And I'd ask my parents if we could live with them for a year if Grace's hours were cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly for her. Like watching someone walk on ice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the school made AI compulsory for reports, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it, grumbling. I'm not going to lose my job over a report template. But I'd still write the comments on the kids I know properly myself, because parents can tell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the church. My dad's a builder and he's always said there's a room for us. The vicar's wife runs a food bank and I never thought I'd say this, but I'd rather lean on my family and the church than fill in a government form.

I'd want **parents** to decide what their children use, not tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is reckless, and the people who built it without asking anyone should answer for it. I'd say families and churches will have to hold things together. I'd still be wary of the government making it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think history teaching as a paid job is finished by 2028 at a small school like ours. The AI could teach the Romans better than me and mark every essay in seconds. What's left is keeping teenagers safe in a room, and they'd pay someone less for that. Grace's job would go first. With less than a month in the bank, we'd be in trouble by Easter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding, or do it at the registry office with ten people. We'd move in with my parents. I'd ask my dad to take me on as a builder's labourer, because hands-on work gives us about three years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the night my grandad died, when everything you assumed about next week stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You never use AI. Would you start in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe at school if they made me. But I wouldn't put my life into learning it, because by 2028 it doesn't need me to learn it, it just does the job. My time's better spent learning to plaster a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my fiancée Grace that a marriage is the vows, not the party. I'd mean it, but I'd still be sad. Her mum's bought a hat already.

say: I'd call it **reckless** and say its builders should answer for it.
I'd say **families and churches** will hold things together.

With **less than a month** saved, they'd be in trouble by Easter.

Work as a **builder's labourer** for his dad.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the night his grandad died.
S2.quote: My time's better spent learning to plaster a wall.
fieldNote: Gareth expects to **lose his job** and his fiancée's too.
He'd use the **robot gap** by switching to building work with his dad.
Learning AI feels **pointless** to him if it does the whole job.

steps.text: Hold the wedding at the registry office with ten guests
Move into his parents' house to save rent
Work as a labourer for his dad's building firm
Ask the church food bank for help if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to think, and schools shouldn't rush. I'd want parents and churches to have a say. I'd say it at the parents' evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years feels worse than you'd think, because it's long enough to start a family and too short to know if I'll have a job. I'd be thirty-two when the thinking part goes. I'm not good at switching, and I don't know what I'd switch to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep the wedding as planned, maybe smaller. I'd start learning building work with my dad on Saturdays, slowly, so I've got something. And Grace and I would put off having children for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed underneath. Like knowing there's a storm forecast for the wedding day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off children. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. Family is the point of all of it for me. But I won't bring a child into a house with no income, and my parents never did that to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Grace's job over five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The surgery would switch her job to a computer well before 2031. She's already scared of the new booking system they put in. Grace thinks about training as a dental nurse, which is hands-on, but that's two years and money we haven't got.

say: I'd say **five years** gives time to think, so schools shouldn't rush.
I'd want **parents and churches** to have a say.
think: Five years is long enough to start a family but too short to know about **his job**.
He's **not good at switching** and doesn't know what to switch to.
do: Keep teaching and keep a **smaller wedding**.
Learn **building work** with his dad on Saturdays.
Put off **having children** for a few years.
feel: **Alarmed** underneath, like a storm forecast for the wedding day.
S3.quote: I won't bring a child into a house with no income, and my parents never did that to me.
fieldNote: The middle timeline **troubles Gareth most** emotionally, because of family plans.

steps.text: Learn plastering and building with his dad on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives families and schools time, and I'd hope we use it to protect what matters. I'd say children need teachers who know them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough to breathe. I'd be thirty-seven, married, maybe with a child. I think small schools would still want teachers for a while, especially church schools where parents want a person. But my pay won't grow much, and that's the hard bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching, get married next August as planned, and start a family in two or three years. I'd try to become head of humanities, which means more pay. And I'd keep the building work as a backup over the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a normal way. Like any young couple with a mortgage they can't get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said parents want a person. Are you sure about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm sure about ours. Our parents drive past a bigger school to send their children here because of the chapel and because we know the kids' names. That won't change in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try AI tools in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe once the head insisted and others had been using them for years. I'd be the last one, and proud of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. It takes my job and Grace's before we've even married. What would help is time, and support for families, not just cash, like apprenticeships for people my age so I can learn a trade properly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people round here would get through this because they've got a church and neighbours. Nobody talks about that in these AI debates.
